## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction

 Big Picture

No Child Left Behind

 NCLB requirements for testing have left states buried in data
 with mandates to use the data to improve education.
 The most frequently cited mandate is that by 2014 all
 students will perform at a proficient or higher level in reading
 and math.
 Concern that this mandate is unrealizable has led some
 experts to propose modifying NCLB’s AYP criteria to
 incorporate student growth.
 [Kingsbury et al., 2004, Hill, 2003, Thum, 2003]
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/05.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 No Child Left Behind
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Important Considerations
 Standards Based Growth
 Institutional or Individual Growth
 Big Picture

No Child Left Behind

 NCLB requirements for testing have left states buried in data
 with mandates to use the data to improve education.
 The most frequently cited mandate is that by 2014 all
 students will perform at a proficient or higher level in reading
 and math.
 Concern that this mandate is unrealizable has led some
 experts to propose modifying NCLB’s AYP criteria to
 incorporate student growth.
 [Kingsbury et al., 2004, Hill, 2003, Thum, 2003]
 Linn (2004), for example, suggests a combination of
 longitudinal student analysis with an annual NCLB-like status
 measure.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/09.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 No Child Left Behind
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Important Considerations
 Standards Based Growth
 Institutional or Individual Growth
 Big Picture

Important Considerations

 The primary goal of longitudinal data analysis should be to
 return worthwhile information that informs, refines, alters, and
 ultimately improves practice.
 Currently, standards are the lingua franca of instruction,
 assessment, and accountability.
 For growth analyses to be both understandable and useful,
 they should synchronize with these standards.
 The purpose of this presentation is to better situate current
 analyses of longitudinal data within the context of
 performance standards.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/10.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 No Child Left Behind
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Important Considerations
 Standards Based Growth
 Institutional or Individual Growth
 Big Picture

No Child Left Behind
Institutional or Individual Growth

 NCLB’s AYP mandates stipulate growth. The growth,
 however, is institutional instead of individual. For example,
 next year’s 5th grade should outperform this year’s 5th grade.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/11.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 No Child Left Behind
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Important Considerations
 Standards Based Growth
 Institutional or Individual Growth
 Big Picture

No Child Left Behind
Institutional or Individual Growth

 NCLB’s AYP mandates stipulate growth. The growth,
 however, is institutional instead of individual. For example,
 next year’s 5th grade should outperform this year’s 5th grade.
 If cohorts are identical from year-to-year, then NCLB based
 growth will likely imply institutional improvement.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/12.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 No Child Left Behind
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Important Considerations
 Standards Based Growth
 Institutional or Individual Growth
 Big Picture

No Child Left Behind
Institutional or Individual Growth

 NCLB’s AYP mandates stipulate growth. The growth,
 however, is institutional instead of individual. For example,
 next year’s 5th grade should outperform this year’s 5th grade.
 If cohorts are identical from year-to-year, then NCLB based
 growth will likely imply institutional improvement.
 A second way to assess institutional improvement is to ensure
 that the “amount” students learn in a given grade increases
 over time. That is, for a given grade, there is an increasing
 rate of change in student growth.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/13.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 No Child Left Behind
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Important Considerations
 Standards Based Growth
 Institutional or Individual Growth
 Big Picture

No Child Left Behind
Institutional or Individual Growth

 NCLB’s AYP mandates stipulate growth. The growth,
 however, is institutional instead of individual. For example,
 next year’s 5th grade should outperform this year’s 5th grade.
 If cohorts are identical from year-to-year, then NCLB based
 growth will likely imply institutional improvement.
 A second way to assess institutional improvement is to ensure
 that the “amount” students learn in a given grade increases
 over time. That is, for a given grade, there is an increasing
 rate of change in student growth.
 A fundamental question is how to relate individual growth to
 NCLB conceived institutional growth.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/17.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Overview
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Value-Added Analysis
 Standards Based Growth
 Teacher/School Comparisons
 Big Picture

Longitudinal Data Analysis

 Annual state testing of students provides mountains of
 longitudinal data.
 The most prominent type of longitudinal analysis currently
 employed on student data are the value-added analyses
 developed by Dr. William Sanders.
 In education, value-added analysis is synonymous with
 longitudinal analysis of data.
 Using this familiarity as a starting point, consider two basic
 questions:
 Value-added by whom/what?
 Value-added relative to what?

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/19.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Overview
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Value-Added Analysis
 Standards Based Growth
 Teacher/School Comparisons
 Big Picture

Value-Added by Whom/What?

 Usually the value-added inference is to the teacher or school.
 The term teacher effect implies that teacher actions are
 responsible for a given effect. That is, that the teacher caused
 the effect.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/20.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Overview
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Value-Added Analysis
 Standards Based Growth
 Teacher/School Comparisons
 Big Picture

Value-Added by Whom/What?

 Usually the value-added inference is to the teacher or school.
 The term teacher effect implies that teacher actions are
 responsible for a given effect. That is, that the teacher caused
 the effect.
 Determination of cause usually requires random assignment.
 For example, in determining whether a particular curriculum is
 effective, the gold standard employs random assignment of
 subjects to treatment in the form of an experimental design.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/21.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Overview
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Value-Added Analysis
 Standards Based Growth
 Teacher/School Comparisons
 Big Picture

Value-Added by Whom/What?

 Usually the value-added inference is to the teacher or school.
 The term teacher effect implies that teacher actions are
 responsible for a given effect. That is, that the teacher caused
 the effect.
 Determination of cause usually requires random assignment.
 For example, in determining whether a particular curriculum is
 effective, the gold standard employs random assignment of
 subjects to treatment in the form of an experimental design.
 There is a great deal of debate as to whether value-added
 analyses using observational data can accurately estimate the
 contribution by whom/what [Rubin et al., 2004].

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/22.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Overview
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Value-Added Analysis
 Standards Based Growth
 Teacher/School Comparisons
 Big Picture

Value-Added Relative to What?

 Even if one can validly attribute responsibility for a measured
 effect to a teacher/school, just what does the effect mean?

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/23.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Overview
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Value-Added Analysis
 Standards Based Growth
 Teacher/School Comparisons
 Big Picture

Value-Added Relative to What?

 Even if one can validly attribute responsibility for a measured
 effect to a teacher/school, just what does the effect mean?
 Value-added usually denotes residual performance above (or
 below) a statistically determined expectation.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/24.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Overview
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Value-Added Analysis
 Standards Based Growth
 Teacher/School Comparisons
 Big Picture

Value-Added Relative to What?

 Even if one can validly attribute responsibility for a measured
 effect to a teacher/school, just what does the effect mean?
 Value-added usually denotes residual performance above (or
 below) a statistically determined expectation.
 What does growth above expectation represent in terms of
 standards based performance?

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/25.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Overview
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Value-Added Analysis
 Standards Based Growth
 Teacher/School Comparisons
 Big Picture

Value-Added Relative to What?

 Even if one can validly attribute responsibility for a measured
 effect to a teacher/school, just what does the effect mean?
 Value-added usually denotes residual performance above (or
 below) a statistically determined expectation.
 What does growth above expectation represent in terms of
 standards based performance?
 An answer to this question greatly enhances the
 interpretability and utility with respect to current standards
 based accountability initiatives.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

```{=html}
Value Added Relative to What?
```

```{=html}
 There is an incongruence between many presently used growth
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/30.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Overview
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Value-Added Analysis
 Standards Based Growth
 Teacher/School Comparisons
 Big Picture

Value Added Relative to What?

 For a teacher adding value significantly above (or below) the
 district average, what can be expected of this teacher’s
 students in terms of performance standards?
 There is an incongruence between many presently used growth
 models and NCLB.
 NCLB achievement mandates are standards based.
 Growth models that rely upon scale scores return normative
 comparisons.
 If normative results for students are inadequate, why should
 normative comparisons of teachers be any different?

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/31.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Overview
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Value-Added Analysis
 Standards Based Growth
 Teacher/School Comparisons
 Big Picture

Which Growth Metric
Scale Scores or Performance Standards

 Scale Score Based Growth
 Conceptually simple interval scale based results.
 Scale score based results require translation to standards
 based criteria.
 Difficult to define “how much growth” is enough without
 normative references.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/32.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Overview
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Value-Added Analysis
 Standards Based Growth
 Teacher/School Comparisons
 Big Picture

Which Growth Metric
Scale Scores or Performance Standards

 Scale Score Based Growth
 Conceptually simple interval scale based results.
 Scale score based results require translation to standards
 based criteria.
 Difficult to define “how much growth” is enough without
 normative references.
 Standards Based Growth
 Conceptually simple probability based results.
 Amenable to standards based accountability initiatives.
 Simple to define “how much growth” with regard to
 NCLB-like policy mandates.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

```{=html}
Standards Based Growth

 Change (growth) is modeled via student movement between
 performance categories.
 Student movement can refer to annual change.
 Student movement can refer to long term change. For
 example, between the beginning and end of middle school
 Growth estimates are quantified as transition probabilities.
 That is, the probability of observing a transition between
 performance categories.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

```{=html}
 chance for a student to remain at the
 .3 highest performance level.
 Similarly, there might be a 50%
 PL3
 chance of moving from the lowest to
 the next to lowest category.
 These conditions impose constraints
 PL2
 upon two other performance level
 .5
 transitions.

 .5 PL1

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/77.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Summary
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Goals
 Standards Based Growth
 References
 Big Picture

Summary

 When measuring growth, the choice of metric impacts the results
 of the analyses and their interpretation.
 Scale Scores
 Growth analyses using scale scores often yield results in
 that metric.
 The abstract nature of the scale requires interpretation of
 results to be based in normative comparisons.
 Results are not congruent with many standards based
 accountability initiatives.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/78.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Introduction
 Summary
 Longitudinal Analysis of Student Data
 Goals
 Standards Based Growth
 References
 Big Picture

Summary

 When measuring growth, the choice of metric impacts the results
 of the analyses and their interpretation.
 Performance Standards
 Growth analyses using performance standards yield
 results in that metric.
 Transitions between performance categories are
 interpretable without recourse to normative comparisons.
 Results are easily mapped onto current standards based
 accountability initiatives.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```

```{=html}
 The natural way to analyze the question is to look at
 movement between performance levels.
 Transition probabilities locate growth within NCLB mandates
 and map directly back to performance standards around which
 curriculum and instruction are based.

 D. W. Betebenner Performance Standards and Growth</div>
```
